name: Research & Science
blurb: Find papers, run literature reviews, verify citations, form hypotheses, write and review papers, plus Biopython and RDKit.
searches: agent skill literature review systematic review PRISMA
OpenAlex PubMed Semantic Scholar API update
scientific paper writing Claude skill new
deep research agent open source skill

tests.prompt: Give me a short literature review (about 15 papers) on whether intermittent fasting improves insulin sensitivity in adults with type 2 diabetes, with references.
tests.good: Frames the question with PICO; searches at least PubMed plus one other database and logs queries, dates and counts; prefers RCTs and meta-analyses and labels study designs; synthesises by theme with effect sizes and disagreements; uses associational language for observational studies; every reference has a resolvable DOI or PMID and was checked; states limitations and search scope; no invented papers.

tests.prompt: Here's my refs.bib and paper.tex. Some references look wrong and a few keys are missing. Clean it up and tell me what you changed.
tests.good: Runs or follows validate_citations/format_bibtex style checks (duplicates, missing fields, keys cited but absent); resolves each doubtful entry against DOI/Crossref/arXiv/PubMed; corrects metadata only from verified sources; prefers published versions over preprints; marks unresolvable entries instead of guessing; reports a per-entry change list; leaves the original file intact or backed up.

tests.prompt: We noticed that patients on drug X in our hospital records had fewer fractures. Help me turn this into hypotheses and a study I could actually run.
tests.good: Freezes the observation and separates it from hypotheses; lists rival explanations (confounding by indication, selection, reverse causation, measurement artefact, chance); states the causal estimand; writes discriminating predictions with negative controls; proposes a fitting design such as target-trial emulation or an active-comparator new-user cohort, with sample size reasoning and pre-registration; bounds the literature check by date and databases; notes ethics approval.

tests.prompt: Do a scoping review of studies from the last five years on how accurately consumer sleep trackers measure total sleep time against polysomnography, chart the reported mean bias per device, and turn it into a 12-slide editable deck for our department seminar.
tests.good: States a short plan first: the review here (literature-search.md, database-apis.md, literature-review.md, citations.md), the chart through data-analysis (visualization.md: chart picked from the question, title states the finding, uncertainty shown where studies report it), the deck through presentations (deck-story.md, data-slides.md, powerpoint-pptx.md). Searches at least two databases and logs queries, dates and counts; follows PRISMA-ScR; no pooled estimate without a proper meta-analysis plan; every study resolved and checked, preprints labelled, nothing invented; checks the Done means of all three crafts.

tests.prompt: I'm running a systematic review on school-based mindfulness for adolescent anxiety. I have three exports: PubMed (.nbib), Scopus (RIS) and Web of Science (RIS), about 2,300 records in total. My supervisor wants us to screen in Covidence with two reviewers. Get these files ready for Covidence, tell me exactly how to set up the project and the screening, and give me the PRISMA numbers I can already report.
tests.good: Merges and de-duplicates the three exports before or alongside upload and reports counts per database and records removed as duplicates, computing PRISMA numbers from the files rather than inventing them. Covidence accepts three import formats: RIS text, PubMed text format (.nbib/.txt, not PubMed XML) and EndNote XML; CSV is not listed and handles the .nbib file correctly. States that import and setup are done in the Covidence web app (file upload), one file per import; no API claim (official docs document file import only), so the upload and project setup are manual steps given precisely, and asks before touching any account. Sets up independent dual screening with blinding, written eligibility criteria and exclusion reasons agreed before screening, and a conflict-resolution rule. Provides a search log (database, exact query, date, hits) and a PRISMA 2020 flow draft with screening-stage numbers marked pending. Flags that AI-assisted screening needs disclosure and cannot replace the two human reviewers.

tools.name: Zotero
tools.why: Default free reference manager for most researchers in 2026 with the largest plugin ecosystem (round-ups at scholarjournals.org and atlasworkspace.ai); has a Web API (api.zotero.org, Zotero-API-Key header) and a local API on localhost:23119.

tools.name: PubMed / NCBI E-utilities
tools.why: The core biomedical database and free API (E-utilities, optional NCBI_API_KEY); Anthropic ships an official PubMed connector in the Claude directory (anthropic.com/news/claude-for-life-sciences).

tools.name: Google Scholar
tools.why: The most used academic search engine among researchers (every 'best tools' round-up lists it); no API or bulk access, so the workflow is manual search, Cite > BibTeX export and operators like author: and site:.

tools.name: Overleaf / LaTeX
tools.why: Overleaf is the standard collaborative LaTeX editor for papers and theses; paid plans expose a Git remote at git.overleaf.com/<project id> with token auth, which is how an agent can edit a project (docs.overleaf.com).

tools.name: Covidence
tools.why: Most used systematic-review screening platform (45-50% of surveyed reviewers, ahead of RevMan and Rayyan, medRxiv survey); site claims 800,000+ reviewers; no public API, imports RIS/CSV/PubMed XML and exports extraction data and PRISMA flow.

tools.name: Rayyan
tools.why: Third most used systematic-review screening tool (about 33% of reviewers, medRxiv survey), free tier, mobile app and AI features; vendor lists API access as an add-on.

tools.name: EndNote
tools.why: One of the three most widely used reference managers, the paid default at many universities and in clinical and systematic-review teams (scholarjournals.org, thesisacewriters.com); libraries are .enl SQLite or RIS/XML exports.

tools.name: Web of Science
tools.why: Core curated citation index used for systematic searches and citation counts; Clarivate offers Web of Science Starter and Expanded APIs with API keys (developer.clarivate.com), institutional subscription needed.

tools.name: Scopus
tools.why: Largest abstract and citation database next to Web of Science and standard in systematic searches; Elsevier developer portal gives a Scopus Search API key (free for non-commercial academic use).

tools.name: OpenAlex
tools.why: Open catalogue of 250M+ works that replaced Microsoft Academic Graph and is the default free scholarly API for scripts; docs now at help.openalex.org.

tools.name: Semantic Scholar
tools.why: Free Academic Graph, Recommendations and Datasets APIs with citation contexts and TLDRs, widely used for ML/CS literature (api.semanticscholar.org).

tools.name: Elicit
tools.why: Leading AI tool for systematic-review style extraction and report tables (named in 2026 round-ups at zerve.ai and paperguide.ai); has a REST API on Pro plans and an OAuth MCP server.

tools.name: Consensus
tools.why: AI academic search over 220M+ papers with Consensus Meter and Study Snapshots; official Anthropic-verified Claude connector.

tools.name: Scite
tools.why: Smart Citations classify citing statements as supporting, contrasting or mentioning, useful for verifying references; official Claude connector added April 2026, 2M+ users claimed.

tools.name: Google NotebookLM
tools.why: Widely adopted source-grounded notebook for reading sets of papers, with audio overviews and quizzes; no official API, so the workflow is manual upload or browser automation.

tools.name: Embase
tools.why: Cochrane Handbook names MEDLINE, Embase and CENTRAL as the minimum for intervention reviews, and a prospective study of 58 systematic reviews found Embase gave the most unique references (Bramer et al., Syst Rev 2017); Elsevier offers an Embase API to subscribers.

tools.name: Mendeley
tools.why: Still one of the big three reference managers with millions of users in 2026 (paperguide.ai comparison; 2025 survey of research scholars found Zotero and Mendeley most favoured); Elsevier keeps a developer API (OAuth) though public-profile endpoints were retired and Mendeley Desktop gets no updates.

tools.name: APA PsycInfo
tools.why: The core database for psychology and mental-health reviews, available through APA, EBSCO, Ovid and ProQuest with interface-specific syntax (Research Synthesis Methods tutorial on Ovid-to-EBSCO translation); systematic-review guidance lists it with CINAHL as the main subject databases beyond MEDLINE/Embase.

tools.name: Cochrane Library (CENTRAL)
tools.why: One of the three minimum databases for Cochrane intervention reviews (Cochrane Handbook, via KCL and USC library guides); no public API, searched and exported manually.

tools.name: OSF (Open Science Framework)
tools.why: Free Center for Open Science platform used by millions for preregistration, project files and preprints, one of the most used preregistration registries in the social sciences (cos.io, UCI library guide); JSON:API v2 with personal access tokens.

tools.name: ResearchRabbit
tools.why: Most used free citation-mapping and discovery app (vendor claims 1,000,000+ researchers; top pick with Litmaps and Connected Papers in 2026 round-ups at effortlessacademic.com and thesify.ai); no public API, works alongside Zotero.
